blocks.x: I don't know. Some of the fellows in the band seem like it's in the green. He pulled out and he organized the Excelsior band.
It had been called the Creole band.
Yeah, yeah. It had been called the Creole band.
Mr. Valero, we might, as we start the tape, we'd like to get your name, the right spelling and your full name on the tape so that we can identify the tape.
My sightings are very good. I have to wear glasses, but I can see how I write down here and give you money.
And also just when you were born and if it was right here in Mobile, just where you came from.
Let me see. I'll put my name. Thank you.
I saw Mr. Pope in, it was about the 1st of May, I believe, several months ago, and I intended to come back and try to see you a few weeks later, but I didn't get over until today. I didn't get over.
You want my aid, you say?
Yes, just your birth date, if you can just tell us. You can just tell us. It'll be on the tape and we can take it down later. You don't have to write it down. It's all right.
Let's see. 81. You want me to speak now? Yes, you can. What is your full name?
William Edward Valerio. William E. Valerio. And how is that spelled?
B-A-L-L-A-I-E-L.
B-A-L-L-A-I-L. I-E-L. Valerio. Valerio. I thought it was something like Valero, like the Spanish dance. I didn't know the spelling.
And my birth date is 11th of October. I was born in 1881.
1881. Uh-huh. So how old are you now? You're about...
And my next birthday this month, 11th of this month, I'll be 78 years old. 78. 78. Uh-huh. That's the day before Columbus Day. Oh, yes.
You were telling us the band had been called the Creole Band at first?

It was called the Creole Band years ago. That's what I learned from the old folks, you know. Uh-huh. And then, uh, with this little disagreement, uh, this Alec Pope, this, uh, John Pope's father, he organized Excelsa Band. Uh-huh. And then, let's say, he got some of the fellas to pull with him and he organized an Excelsa Band. Uh-huh. And then the Excelsa Band, uh, with, uh, with, uh, the old Creole Band, it, it lived, uh, around, I guess, around 70 years, you see. Yeah. Yeah. And I joined it, oh, let's see, when did I join it? I can't even just remember. But anyway.
I was going to ask, I don't even know which instruments you played or if you played more than one.
Well, I played several different instruments. When I first joined the band, I was playing cornet, you see.
What was the first instrument? When you were a boy, what instrument did you start?

Well, I didn't, I played, I was a grown man when I was a guy, learned to brass instruments. You really did. When I was a boy, I played string instruments. Oh, you did? By air, you see. But when I joined the band, I played by note and played brass instruments by note. And that was way back, I guess, when I joined the band, back in about, uh, about the twenties, or something, somewhere in the twenties. And, uh, of course, I played in another band before I joined the Excelsior Band. And I stayed in the Excelsior Band maybe in about, uh, twenty-five or thirty years, something like that, you see. Well, anyway, when the band began to dwindle down, they began to die out. The old heads began to die out, you see. And it began to dwindle down until this practice couldn't get good fellas to join, because they had the talent, you know. Yes. And it dwindled on down. So, it, um, all the old, well, we, uh, all those practice, cruel people, you see. Yeah. And, uh, they died out. Then lots of American boys joined in. One would come in after a while, and when another would quit or die, something like that. And still, there's a few fellas that now, they're still carrying that name, you see. Yes, I know. They still have the name. But none of them was none of the old members. None of them was the old members. All these new youngsters was, was got the band now. And, uh, they still carrying that name, the Excelsior Band, that is, in order to get work and things, because the Excelsior Band had everything around them over here. And, uh, it, uh, had a good reputation, and I mean, from, uh, I guess, from New Orleans, a little up Chicago, Pensacola, everywhere. There were people in New Orleans, especially in New Orleans.
Yes, over there, they talk about them, yeah. Yeah, yeah, yeah.

And, uh, when I joined it, uh, they, they kind of appointed me as secretary, and I kept a record of the, of the jobs we'd play, and what we got out the job, and what each man received, and so on. And, uh, I was, I was the only one, however, with the secretary that locked things down, you see, the fellas, they were kind of be a, a paymaster, received them on in, to pay off, or something like that, but they never would keep a record of what the band was doing, you see. Yes, that's very interesting. But when I, when I went in, I was taking it on myself, and this book is old, so, uh, the last man that died, that's Johnny Pope's uncle, he was playing bass drum, and he always, um, they were, and, uh, Blair, as long as you live, say, you keep that book, say, that's, that's a nice record that you saw it up, and keep them everything, and, uh, when they wanted to find out, get an argument and anything, you wanted to afford them, uh, anything they were arguing about, and, of course, as far as paying, and, and what they made, and so on, where they played at, well, I had it down in this book, and I could reform to the book and show them, you see.
You have some of the music there, too.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Can I see what pieces they played there? I didn't know this was any of it, see. That might have been some of the music, see.
Oh, look, the first piece we pick up is called New Orleans Jazz.
Yeah, I was crazy about that piece, and I always, I always kept that piece, you see.

Look at that, New Orleans Jazz. Yeah. My Desi left. There's a piece of music, too. One Step by Don Richards, and this happens to be the B-flat soprano sax part. Yeah. Published by Leo Feist. It doesn't give the date. And the other parts are from the same piece, except here's one more number called the Royal Scotch Highlanders, a march. And we have the third and fourth E-flat alto parts. It's by K.L. King. I forget the publisher. The publisher's mark is torn off here.
Now, if those pieces would do you any good, I can mark my name on the back of them, and you can have those.

Well, I'll tell you, let's take one of them anyway. We'll take one, uh... That New Orleans Jazz? ...this one New Orleans Jazz, and we don't want to take all of them, because you might want to give them to somebody else, too.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Now, this here, this here, I don't know about that.
Now, here's the first clarinet part, or the E-flat clarinet.

Well, I didn't play the E-flat, I played the B-flat. I just kept on, you know, just because of, well, remembrance or something. Never been. It might be pieces. I know this is one, I really, really did like that New Orleans Jazz. It's the H-flat.
If you're sure you don't need that. No, I won't need that.
We don't want to take it if you'll be never playing it again. Well, I don't think of my days is too long now.
Well, I hope, I hope you live a long time.

Well, the way I'm feeling, I, I, I feel like I could live over a hundred years old. Right. With the exception of my sight for this big, you see. But I have been, so the doctors gave me up, my wife and all, for just a matter of hours. I had a heart attack about nine years ago, and they're taking me from the church and the ambulance. And so I stayed in the hospital thirteen days. And the doctor and all had given me up for a matter of hours. So, but I pulled through them and I haven't had a setback since I come out. That's good. I've been taking care of my sins.
You also, I notice, have a little booklet here of bugle calls.

Well, that was just as long as the beginners or something. Or anyone on there would like to learn the bugle calls or something. Yes, such as the. You know, to help them in the army or something. Yes. I just, I just put that aside in here.
Yes, I notice it has all of the first call and the assemblies and to the colors and stable to the quarters, taps. Yes, everything.
Now I'm going to put my name and my birthday and all in here if you like. With the, on this piece of music if you like. That'll be fine, yes.
Just your name will be alright because we have your birthday now down on the tape.
I'll give you my full name, William. Yes, that'll be fine.
And this was played by the Excelsior band. William. The other parts here we also found in addition to the carnet part we have the E flat clarinet part. And the B flat tenor sax.
1881. That, that, that shows me. It's coming October, the 70, 70, 70, 80 or so. I'll put this right down here in our briefcase so we won't forget. You want me to put my address on there too?
Oh yes, if you don't mind that'll, because we had a little trouble finding you. Yeah. Up at the cathedral we didn't see you. Then we first went up here to 404, I thought your address is. It's 414.
Is that right? Mm-hmm. Good, so we have your phone number here too.

I'll put that in our briefcase. And here are the other pieces if you want to put that back in your book. I'd like to ask a little bit about the book after a while. Just some of those jobs where you played.
Yeah, if I, if I could see that we were, I'd, you'd have to look at them and stuff. And you can date on back to where I first started.
Oh yes, if you want me to look at it if you don't mind, I'll look at that.
Oh, that's okay.
There's no secret, you see. Yes.
No secret.
It starts in 1917. And does this give the pay that the different people got, like 280?
Yeah, that's what each man would see off the job, you see. Back here would be where you would play that and what to receive for the job.

I noticed here on May the 5th, 1917, you played baseball. Yeah. Is that for a baseball game? Yes, right. And then a Maypole on May the 7th. Yeah. And it looks like carnations ball. Mm-hmm. And a lawn party on the 9th of May. Yeah, that's, you see.

I just walked on where we played at and what you got and while I was secretary and paying off, I just walked on what each man received, you see. And them days, they wasn't paying with music like they're paying for them now, you see. Oh no. Everything was cheap in them days. You made street dollars, you made it for the man's job. Oh yes. We always got our, our good price, you see. Uh-huh. And I discussed this from 1917. Yeah. And that's a little further back there. I thought it was around 1920 when I was. That's 20 what? Back a little further, see.
And the next day on May the 10th, it looks like P.T. Company, 11 Picnic, or P.F. Company, I'm not sure. Well that's some society, you know.
Some society. Yeah.

And then on the 12th of May was the school exercises. Mm-hmm. You only got a dollar sixty-five for those jobs. Yeah, it was just a little, a few hours, a couple hours. And then on the 18th was an outing. Mm-hmm. And the 21st Excelsior Band Picnic. Yeah. And on the 28th was the Sawmill Union. Yeah. And then in June, you, it's a little hard to read all of these because it's faded some. Yeah. Yeah. Looks like Mrs. P. Andrews. Yeah. And then another Excelsior Picnic.
And some other society meeting.
And another picnic on the 11th. About every other day you'd be playing.
Here's another lawn party. Oh, sometimes you'd be playing every night in the week, you see. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Royal Bankers outing. Mm-hmm. I'll read a couple more of these. It's interesting to see all of these different organizations that you played for. Yeah, yeah, yeah. So many of them.
And the Mill looks like the Mill and Kimbers picnic. And it looks like State Street Church picnic. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And another party here. Looks like Nettie Williams or somebody. Yeah. Some lady probably. And another party. And the Zion Church. The Jolly Goodfellows. Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah. And there's another society here that I can't make out for sure. A picnic. And the Jolly Goodfellows. This Jolly Goodfellows had two outings in July. Another lawn party in July. Well, there's a note here that you purchased the horn. Yeah. On July 31st, 1917.

Now, you see, people in order to get the Excelsior Band, draw a crowd, they did sign up jobs with us sometimes from this year to the next year, you see. Take that same date on a big holiday or something like that. All the people that we'd play for regularly, you know, they'd sign up from one year to the other, you know, to get the Excelsior Band. Yeah. Because they know the Excelsior Band's on the crowd, you see. Right.

And here's some more organizations. I'll read a few of these since you say you have trouble reading them now. There's a boiler helpers company. That's one. Here's one I can't quite make up. It looks like demonstration of something for boys. It says Mineta there too on the end of the line.
I wonder what that was. If I could see you in my glasses.
Here's a public ball on April the 29th. This is the next year I'm reading now. It's interesting to see all of these different, here's the Red Cross parade.
Yeah.
And another ball.
Football and baseball and all that.

Here's an exhibition drill at some school. Subscription boy outing, boiler helpers again. And the longshoremen picnic. Yeah. And here's on May the 30th of that year's Decoration National Cemetery. All sorts of schools and clubs and picnics.
You want to use this? I'll have to use this sometime. Oh, no. That's all right. If there's anything that you want to say. No, I didn't know nothing particular. I just wanted to.
Here's a sawmill union picnic.

Just all sorts of organizations. Mozart Club, must have been a music club, was it? Well, I guess it was. All kinds of clubs. Good Shepherd Grill. That gives us a very good idea of the sort of organizations you played.
You see how much work we would have.

There's Ladies' Society, an industrial, Ladies' Industrial Society, Zion Church, Mobile Shipbuilders, just every sort of an organization that you could think of it looks like here, as I look over the list, just unlimited number of different organizations.
That's a fine book.
And the prices you usually received was in around $2 all the way to $2.15, $2.30 quite often. Sometimes $2.55. Occasionally you'd get as much as $4.

I didn't drop it. We had $2.50 or $3.00 for an hour. The musicians and I were getting $10, $12, $15 for them. Yeah, that's right. They'd only go out now. Most of us are orchestras around here now. There's no brass bands around there except them few fellows was trying to hold up the Excelsis' name during the connoisseur time. They'd get some work. But otherwise, there's all orchestras around here now. And them fellows that get $10, $12, $15 every time they go out and play. They'd play sometime, extra hours at night, they'd come back with $20, $25 each in their
pocket.

Yeah, the orchestra's getting good money around here now. In fact, everybody's getting good money except them. Yes, that's right. Poor common labor. He's doing pretty good too. But they're getting better pay now than they ever get it since mobile or been a mobile. Since the South has been a South of them.

I guess so. Here's one that's interesting, 1919. I never did know when they celebrated the Emancipation Parade. It was on January the 1st. That's right, that's right. Paid $2.85. See if there's any other Excelsior band ball. Did you put on those dances yourself?

Well, yeah, the ball. And sometimes we'd, well, them ball would pay, we'd have a crowded house. We'd make us six, eight, ten, twelve dollars a piece out there in ball. You see, we'd be so proud they couldn't only dance in them. They'd do the NHL so bad. Especially around carnival time. We played all the parades and practically all the balls we could play for the white people. And in the evening, the Mardi Gras evening, we'd take about two, three hours after the day parade and give a ball for ourselves. We'd play around $20 a piece out of ball.
That's good. That's fine. Here's the Spanish-American soldiers and another dance in February of 1919. Several other organizations. The Easter dance that year in April, and the Easter picnic.

There wasn't a club or no organization or anything that was a drama or build. We didn't play music for it. Except we had plenty of it. It was a while. It was worse sometimes. I've seen times too that we'd go on a job for some speaking or something. They'd do mostly speaking. We'd play about three tunes, you see, and get paid out full money for it, you see. It was all that.
I see sometimes you got paid as much as four dollars. Yeah, there's one a little over four dollars.
We made high, ten, twelve, fifteen dollars off a job, you know, just playing a few hours. So I'm calling what the jobs was and where they were. We'd play out the city and in the city.
You usually average about a dozen engagements a month, it looks like here. That would be three a week, maybe.
Well, we'd get more than that, lots of that.
Here in May, every day, look in May of 1919, I believe it's every day. Hardly skip a day. That's when the baseball season started.
Yeah, and the picnic season, you see.
Did you play for the baseball games?
Oh yeah, I played for the football games, football games, horse races when they come in.
That baseball, was that the southern league for the Mobile team?

No, no, that's the Mobile League, the city league. The city league. Were those some colored teams or white teams or what were they? Well, white teams, mostly white teams, yeah. And then we played for a few colored teams too. Football too.
This is certainly an interesting book. Here's Labor Day Parade in September. There's just so many of them, we won't take time to read all of them.
No, it takes quite a while. You can see that we had plenty of work, you see, according to that book.

Let's see, as the years go on here, sometimes the pay is going up a little bit too. There's more $6 dates here for some of the parties. Up to $6.25 quite often here. That's in the summer too. I'm wondering if you can tell us, Mr. Ballero, about the music when you first began playing. When you were a boy, before you joined any brass band, what was the dance music like here in Mobile? As far back as you can remember, did they have bands with blowing instruments or just strings? What kind of a band did they use?

Well, I think there were a few orchestras around there, but not really. The old time when the boys were coming up, they had most of what they called string bands. It would be string instruments with about maybe four, five, six pieces. But in the late years, after the Excelsior Band, well, during the Excelsior Band, about, I say about 20 years ago, they began to get orchestras together. The fellas began to organize good string orchestras, you see. They'd have pianos and trumpets and clarinet and violins and bass violins and all that. They had regular orchestras like they got now, you see. In my boyhood there, with most musicians around there, there wasn't much pay jobs, you see. It wasn't much pay jobs like it was in the late days where people could make some money out of giving dances and picnics. But in the early days, it was just almost, we'd have string bands and many times we'd go playing the way just to be playing for nothing, you see. Just to be playing for nothing. Yes, enjoy it. Have fun, get our beer and wine or something like that. And we'd play for nothing. And I'd borrow it there, because I'd play mandolin, I'd play guitar, bass, violin, and I could hit a tune on piano. And my wife's piano had been there for years. Well, I see you're moving in the piano. Yeah, she used to play the piano. Did your wife play for the dances too in the U.S.? Well, no, she never did go out for dances. She just played horn, yeah. And in this house, I guess it was around 80 some odd years old, and we had many dances in here with string music and brass music. Yeah, I was thinking, this tool on the chimney and having it relined it, you see. Oh, yes. The class began to fall after 80 some odd years. Yeah. And this was our father's house.
Well, I thought you were just maybe moving in here the way it's being reminded.
No, no, we had it relined it. We had it painted up a couple years ago all on the outside.
So you lived here for years? Yeah, yeah.

I see. And this is our father's homestead, our father's mother's homestead, my wife. And so this house, I guess, in its eight, it was close to 90 years. And all that lumber in there, solid, with the exception of the class, that began to get weak. And so it's having it all re-enined it now, you see. Yes. Putting solitaire at the top and sheetrock and putting that flow on it. This is as good and solid as this flow on top. Right now, that lumber is like a piece of oak under there. It's a pine lumber, you see.

This music fell out of your book. I was going to ask a little bit more about the kind of the music. I know the instruments now you've played. What was the music like? What pieces? Was it like ragtime? Did you ever play the music?

Well, yeah. When I first joined the band, they were just playing straight music, because some of our teachers, they didn't like the ragtime stuff, you see. They wanted us to just play straight music. They didn't want us to put no foolishness in it. Did they play waltzes or marching or poppers or what kind of... Oh, yeah. Pocers, all right. They played waltzes and pokers and quadrilles, mazooka quadrilles, waltz quadrilles and all that, and lances. They had all that for the picnics, you see, in them young days. But they cut them kind of square dances out in the late days. They just got into the fast stuff with the youngsters, you know, you see. They danced all kinds of ways. And we could have some pretty dances around the world, you know. The cut out and the shimmy shiwabbles and all such as that. And, uh, well they had names for them. And they'd have dances that, uh, you'd get in this picnic ground where there's a large stage. And they'd all get, each man gave him a lady partner and get in line, you know, one behind the other and have them dances with the cut out and they'd all do the same thing at the same time, turn the same way. And it was really pretty. Go around the ring, you know, around the ring. It was really pretty. They had some pretty dances. Yeah. And, uh, so they began to get the, the, the, what you say, the kind of fast music playing and jazz music. And then, I don't know, time now they got into the, some other name they got now for the music, the quick tonguing and all that and all kinds of fruits. And sometimes they'd be playing, playing the piece. The one was doing the cutting up when he was on, that would be most of the corn acts or the, or the, or the crowd. The one was doing all the foolishness. It seemed like he wasn't playing nothing but the other fellows would be keeping a nice time. But when he'd stop, he'd be right in there with them, right on, right on the note there with them, you see.
When did that, uh, kind of music come in, that jazzing and all, as you said, that foolishness, all those different variations. When did they start doing that here?
Well that, that, that, that's been about, uh, how about, uh, fifteen, twenty years ago, or eighteen, twenty years ago.
I wonder, did you ever hear any of the bands from New Orleans? Did they come over here? Did you hear any of the New Orleans musicians?

New Orleans bands? I, I remember one when I was quite young, I believe I heard one, but I don't, I don't know whether I was playing music then. But we did have Picnicoria with the Wise band from Pensacola and they, they were supposed to have one of the classic, the best colored bands there was in the south. That is, the real down straight playing music, you see. They didn't put no foolishness in their music, you see. They had won several prizes up in Chicago playing with them, yeah. What was the name band you said? The Wise band. It was an old band named Wise, I think it was W-Y-E, yes, W-Y-E, double T, it's a wise, the wise. Old trio man, that was a trio man over there too. And they, they won prizes up in the north, they went north and, and, and, and paid for the, you know, exhibitions and things up there. And they won prizes up there. So we, we, we'd go over there and have a picnic once in a while with them and we'd come over, they'd come over here. Now, when we'd have that then, the Wise band, it wasn't the band that they were when they won the prizes, you see. And our band was practically the best band in them days when we got together and, and uh, affiliated with each other and, and swapped towns with picnics and things. Yeah. Well, my band was, was practically the best band in that time. Wise band had, when I was down, it was good, yeah. But they had been one of the best bands that was considered in the south. Now, in the Orleans there came that they had plenty of nice bands all that, but the Wise bands always carried that reputation. And then after them, the Excelsior band carried it, you see. But our band, Wise band, he had about twenty some odd pieces. Our band never did carry over fourteen pieces. I was a small band, but they really played. I'm telling you, you're at the world.
Was this Wise band, the Brass band? Yeah, Brass band.

Brass band. They had an orchestra too, but I don't know what the orchestra was named. But the Wise band was a brass band. And then they played straight music, you know, concert stuff and all that. Well, they didn't do much concert playing, but they were just, they did the old everyday stuff around.
What kind of pieces did you play with the Excelsior band and the other bands you played with even before? What kind of music did you use? Any ragtime? Well, yeah, yeah.

We used ragtime, all kind of time. We mixed it up all kind of way. That's what the people would like about it, you see? And all that foolishness is take with them, you know, and they'd follow their way. And when they mix up that stuff and they'd play it good and they'd sound good, you know. And it wasn't nothing but the Excelsior band anywhere you go in Mobile, practically in the south. From St. Louis on down this way, anyone can tell you the old Mobile Excelsior band. But now it's about gone. There's a few fellas trying to hold up the name during the carnival and carry that name, Excelsior, you know.
Can you tell me about the blues? When was the first time you ever heard anybody sing the blues or play the blues?

The blues, that was when, when Frankie Brown, when I first joined the band, and maybe before I joined the band. Now before I joined the Excelsior band, I began to pick up a little music around there. I got some of the fellas in the Excelsior band, gave me a few lessons. And I joined the band, they got up a little band around there in the Ponkinette band. He was a, he was a man too, he had about six or seven in his family and he had a regular orchestra in his family. He had one sister and about five or six brothers and they organized a regular string orchestra in the family. And he was, he got up a band around there named Ponkinette band, that's when I quite stored it in the brass band. Well I played the Ponkinette band a while and then Lipscomb, he used to play with Dick Sillson, and he, I don't know, for some reason he come out and he organized a band, it's his name, Lipscomb band. Well I went in the Lipscomb band. Well the, Excelsior band, they gave me a few men to dine up and they, they picked the best talent they could find out, the little bands to, to join their band. Were those all brass bands or some of them dance bands? Well there was, there was three brass bands there. No brass. And there's been several brass bands around there, they didn't live long. They used to have an old band there during the Excelsior band time they called the Eureka band. And they, and, and, and, it's, it's a, one time they had to go around there before. Were there stuff

and they just got right down to music and they'd take all the Uyghur bands jobs and everything else. There was one of them but the Excelsior band. There's others that get jobs too once in a while in between. But the Excelsior band had to go, you can see from this book. And that's just when I joined it, you see.
When you took up the brass instruments, which ones did you play mostly?

Yeah, carnet. I was taking it up and playing the carnet. Was that B-flat? B-flat. When I joined the band, Excelsior band, I was playing the carnet but I didn't stay on it long. They put me on the alto, of course they had other men that would take the place, you see. And I joined the band.
Did they have any saxophones in the band? Yeah, they had one or two then. And clarinet's two. Did they use the E-flat or the B-flat clarinet?

Well, I think they used mostly the E-flat, E-flat clarinet. And the carnet's used mostly the B-flat carnet. Of course, the Eureka band, they had one E-flat carnet. But the Excelsior band, all their carnet's was B-flat. They had the solos and the fourth carnet and the second carnet. And they'd have one up a carnet player, they'd put one on the third carnet.
Can you remember when Mr. Pope, Alexander Pope played, did he play the E-flat or the B-flat when you were in the band?

Oh, Alexander Pope, he wasn't in the band. He would take jobs for the band. He didn't play it? Alexander, he had done quit the band and his son had taken it over. Johnny had taken it over. So you never played with Alexander Pope? No, I never played on him. But when he was in the band, he played for my father's funeral. And my father died when I was about eight years old. And he was my father. And the old cruel society called, let's see, what was the name of that society? He was the first member they lost. And the old Excelsior band used to, well we played funerals too. The Excelsior band played all the funerals on there. The society was very, they were members with a brass band, you see.
Oh yes, I wanted to ask a little bit more about the funerals. Did they play slow numbers for the funeral marches or hymns or what kind of music did they use?
I didn't notice any funerals listed in the book. Were there funerals there?
Yeah, I'm just way up here now. Let me go back a little way. You go ahead and talk.
That's alright. What did they do on the funeral? Did they meet at the undertaker's parlor? Were they at the home?

No, they made it to society's hall. Then we just marched with the drum to the corpse house or wherever they were laid out at. March there with the drum. Well, they'd play a few church hymns in a slow way, you know, when the corpse was coming out. And after the corpse would come out, we'd get in line to march to the church, you see. And then we'd play funeral marches from the house to the church. Then when we got... They were real slow? Yeah, well it wasn't too slow, it was real slow, but it was a sad, sad music. It was played in a sad way, you know. Like the funeral marching time, you see. And they never had the drums tune up like they would do playing for a place. The fellas would lower their snare drum down and put the handkerchief on the snare, on the snare, to make it sound dead, you know. Yes, I know. And they'd use the drums that way. And they wouldn't use no cymbal on the bass drums. They'd use just the stick, you see. And play the funeral marches on out to the cemetery. Well, the vans would stay on the outside, the cemetery, while they carried the body inside and buried. And when the society come back out, meet us at the cemetery gate, then we'd march with the real stuff on back to the hall, play any kind of marches, see. Real stuff on back to the hall, yeah.
Did you ever put any funny stuff in there, jazz or?

Yeah, coming back, coming back, yeah. They used to have a piece that they used to play around, you know, in the band that sometimes played, coming from the funeral. I believe it was the name, So Glad You're Gone. That's the name, So Glad You're Gone, you wouldn't go buy no bill no harm. And the band used to play that sometimes, you know, coming back from the grave. But the band saw the body and said, well that's too bad to play that coming back. They just stopped playing that, you know.
Over in New Orleans they used to play Didn't He Ramble sometimes after, you know. Yeah. Or I'm glad you're dead, you rascal, you, things like that.
Well, they wanted to head over here and the name's so glad you're gone.
But the people had a good time then, after it was done.
Oh yeah, well they'd come marching back to the hall and get in this band, you see. Most of the society back to their hall and this band, you get paid off.
Would there be many people following them?

Oh yeah, sometimes there's big, big crowds. Sometimes the northern boys, those young stuts, would come from the north, they had a few to come down to the cemetery, the Maynore Cemetery, in the south here. And they'd come down and the big boys would get to fighting and running with bricks and they'd just so, the cops had to just get at them at the time, you know, and break it up. They'd, boy, they'd really swore bricks and fight each other. Get in the fight. They did that over in New Orleans too sometimes. Yeah, yeah. That's the time. Yeah, we'd play the sad music going and then we'd play any kind of stuff coming back, you see, and marching going back. And the societies, they'd have on the uniforms, what we call the protector societies, such as the protector 12s and 11s and 14s and so on. They'd have on the uniforms, they had a uniform that they'd wear. Some of them would have helmets and with a shirt with their number in it, big 12 in it and black pants. And some of them had red shirts and some of them would have white shirts and black cuffs. And it was really nice. And so finally, I don't know, they stopped playing funerals or the law broke them up from having funerals on Sundays, you see. Most of those societies, they'd have a big membership come out for the funeral and they'd hire a band to make a big show in at the church. They'd put off the funeral, the barrel, from the weekday till the Sundays and have it on Sundays. Oh, I see. You see, on Sundays when everybody would be off and they'd have a big turnout on Sundays. Yeah, look at the crowd.

I noticed here back, I guess it's about 19, 19 or 18, you had some funerals listed here. Different associations, looks like YNR Association Funeral, State Street. YMRA, I believe. And Young Men's Relief Association. Relief Association. That was one of the clubs at the society. Yeah, there was a society in the club too. For burial and all. I was wondering about your band, that was in 1920, these parades, I see. Every year you had the Emancipation Parade, you see, on the first of the years.
Carnival Parade, and the First of July, and everything. There was them holidays where the band would have jobs signed up for a year ahead, you know.
Yes, in February I noticed quite a few balls, and it says Carnival Ball.

Now that's the ball we used to play on the wharf after the night parade on the Mardi Gras night, you see. They played until twelve o'clock, and then they'd throw it down on the kind of length, sort of, at twelve o'clock that night. Yeah. But that was a ball that down me looked like. It used to take up a big space on the wharf. There wasn't no place around there to hold the people. It was a white ball, you see. And I'd need to charge the dollar to come in. And that would go to the Carnival Association for the expenses and things that you see around the city. Did you say that was down on the wharf? Oh, on the wharf. They put a campbells around a big place on the municipal wharf down there. Oh, yes. Right on the river. And then, man, it was down there so cold, man, it was almost freezing. Right there where the water would hit you, we would hit you right off the river. And we'd probably have that ball on every Mardi Gras, you see. Until yet they had a carnival ball down there, but the orchestra plays it now.
Can you tell me about how did the whole brass band play for the dance too?

Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. Used two? We wouldn't split them up that way. Used two drummers, did you? Oh, yeah. Uh-huh. We played dance music as well as we did street music. Same as you did on the street, the same lineup. Yeah, yeah. Lots of on the walls and things, such as the reds and dance music. But every day, one step or two steps a time, while marching and singing. Sometimes we'd play more than one steps and so on and then, and just get plenty of music, all right. How many were in the band did you say?
Fourteen.

We always got fourteen. How many carnets? Well, we cared about four carnets. I believe they had two solos, one first and one second, and they had two out-tores, three out-tores, and a couple trombones, bass and baritone, two drummers, and then the clarinets at the time, you see.
When they marched, who was in front and who was in back?

No, no, they faced four in front. They'd have the two, the bass on the left side, the baritone on the outside in front, and the two trombones in the center. Then behind that would come the altos, then behind that would come the carnets and clarinets, and behind that the drummers, you see, the drummers and the bass. But then the fourteen pieces would give you all the music you were looking for, I'm telling you right now.
What color uniforms did you have?
Well, we always mostly had blue. Blue uniforms. Caps?
Blue, blue caps. I believe Mr. Pope told us that sometime at night parades they'd have lights up on them.

Well, they did that long time ago. Not when you were in the band. No, but one or two of them couldn't see good or something like that. Yes. They couldn't read, couldn't read, memorize the three. Many times playing those night parades and things, you didn't get sufficient lights to see the music. And you'd have to memorize the music. And some of them couldn't do it very well, and I was one that couldn't do it very well. Although, when I was playing alto, I had to draw lights, you see, but fairly connection to see the notes and things.
I noticed in a book, Mr. Malero, that it starts off again in 1939. Did you leave the band for a while?

Yeah, I left the band for a while. I left the band for a while. They made me a band for some instance, and I quit for a while, but they insisted on me coming back and I went back, you see. I wondered too about in the... I stayed in it until I just got tired and went down, going down, so I just stayed in it. So practice going down and on. There's only three of us that played in the late year, a good while back. That's Johnny Pope, myself, and a fellow named Denny Trainor. I think his name's right, his name's Simon, but they called him Denny Trainor and he's out in California. Oh, he's the one that you called Comer, yeah. And on the street was the old, old timers, not the real organizers, but from way back. So on the street was living. Every one of them there, they just buried them, yeah, from last year after the evening, buried a drummer and a bass-song player.
Did you always have the music for all of the pieces or did sometimes you make it up with your head and your head?

No, no, no. They always had the music and then, so after they'd learn it, sometimes they'd put in something extra in there, a little jazz and stuff, you know, when they'd come back. They used to have a dance around there too, they called the Shimmy Swabbles. I've heard that. Yeah, you know, they were always there, Shimmy Swabbles.
How did they use that?
Oh, man, they'd just, the lady and the man all would be just wiggling and all kind of wiggling. They'd cut up, they'd cut up.
Was there any particular music you'd play for a dance like that?

No, we'd just play the ordinary common music, you see. Did you ever play any blues with Excelsior Band? Yeah, yeah, we always had plenty of blues, yeah, plenty of blues. We'd play the blues in a regular way, then we could play it in another decent way, you see. Yeah, they'd put it on. We'd find a gang that likes it to do a regular way, we'd play it right away, you see. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah, play it right away.
Do you remember any of the New Orleans musicians coming over here that you ever heard?
No, but there was a Pickwick band down in Fast and Gold there used to come over, once in a while and have picnics and so on. And I think they were named the Pickwick band.
There was one band they told me used to come over here sometime, the Sam Morgan band.

Do you remember the dance? The dance band? No, I think that was from my time. I might have been a young boy, because I'm pretty old, but I don't remember. I just wondered if you heard those fellows. I believe too that they had a X-Seltz band in New Orleans. They did then, that's right, they had one. There's one other question.
When you learned music, did you have a teacher right away to teach you to read music?

Oh yeah, we always carried a teacher with us, you see. One of the clarinet players was a teacher or a cornet player, you see. Now Pope was the leader, but he wasn't a teacher. A trainer, we had a fellow named Training. This fellow I'm training about in California, his cousin, his cousin was a teacher.
I was going to ask, when you first started on the string instruments, mandolin and the other instruments, guitar, did you have a teacher pick that up yourself?

No, no, I guess I'll pick it up by a year. And I played it pretty well, you see. Figured I used to make right smaller chains and such as that before I started with notes. But when I picked up the brass music, then I started with notes, you see.

Just a couple more questions, then I'll stop bothering you. Oh, that's all right. I wonder about the music in the churches, were you always the Catholic? Oh, you worked in the Catholic Church now. Yeah, I was born in the Catholic Church now. They never of course had the spirituals in the Catholic Church, but I wonder, did you ever hear any of the church music, like the Baptist church music when you were young?
Well, only passing by, it was only passing by. But you know, all churches have some kind of music now, they all have sacred music, they're sacred music. Then one more. And there were stuff with
to pray for funerals, they'd never go inside to pray in the church under no consideration. They'd stop on the outside.
Well did you have that music in New Orleans? The Catholic Church didn't let them have a band on the street for the funeral. Did they do that here?

Yeah, they didn't have the band on the street. For the Catholic funeral? Yeah, if the Catholics wanted it, but they never did go in the church. Yes, I understand. Now my father was Catholic and the Excelsior Band played at his funeral when I was a little boy, you see. And that's when I remember a young Excelsior Band good. And this fellow Johnny Post's father was leader then. And my father was dead, oh my goodness, he's been dead. Just to think I'm about 70 years, because my next boyfriend will be in 70. He died when I was about eight years. He died when he was about the age of 40. And my mother struggled with five children until she got 72. She died at 72.

Had your father played any music? No, no, no. He didn't play any music? No, no. He was just a common laborer. One other question, and then I'll stop, is about the Creole people here. Did they speak the Creole dialect or any language, you know, like French?

Well, some of them did, yeah. The older heads did. But, and coming up in the late days, they didn't take much interest in teaching their children. Did they have any special Creole songs in Creole? Do you remember? Down in Mononville Island they speak it, yeah. They call it the Broken French down there. Which island? Mononville Island. That's just about 18 miles down the road, yeah. Out in the Bay, then. Mononville Island, yeah. I guess you've read of Dauphin Island. Well, it's right, right to the side of Dauphin Island. And the people over there that speak that Creole. Yeah, and the Creole people practically owned the whole island at one time, but now they're sold on several land, but there's many of them down there yet. That's where most of my wife's people's from.
But the Creole people, are they mostly French or some Spanish?

Yeah, they're mixed with French and all. Now, my mother, I've been there as I can learn, she came from down in Nassau somewhere, and she spoke French good. My mother was really speaking French. And her mother, she came from Bordeaux, France, my wife's mother. Bordeaux, France. And that's it, they spoke French good. But the younger ones, the people of Mononville Island, they kept the broken French, I believe. They called it the regular Creole talk down there, and they didn't speak it down there yet. But in the city, yeah, they dropped it somewhere or another, you know, they carried on with their children, so their children never knew. And the undercoastered line, a few words, you know. Bonsoir and so on. Well, we certainly enjoyed talking. Can we shut your mouth and all sorts of things?
You're pregnant, Frank. We certainly enjoyed hearing about the old times. And I was going to ask you about those early string bands. Did they have any drums in there?

Well, they'd have a, they'd have a, what they call a, they'd have a drum with a cymbal on it and a trap. They'd call it a trap drum, you see. Now one man would use both. He'd use his foot with the bass drum, it wouldn't be very loud, you see. And he'd use his hand with the snare drum. They had the drums, yeah, in the orchestra. They have them right now, you see. They got them yet.
I didn't know they had them in those early bands.

Well, yeah, they had them, but that is in the real old time, they didn't have the drums. They just had the mostly string music. And they had bass violins. Now they, now in the orchestra, they use bass horns too, now in the orchestra. They use bass violins and bass horns too.
But they just had the bass violins. They had all the time, they just had the bass violins.

And so, Mobiliar's had a good many musicians. Now we got, we got a couple of boys from Mobiliar. One's over in England somewhere, he was a little fella. He picked up around here and was in the Lipskins band. Well, he practically wasn't exactly in the band, he'd just go along with them and play a little at the time. And one of the fellas was taking interest in him and started teaching him the music well. He was playful and he didn't seem to take to it too much. One of them was playing corinette and one of them was playing corn. Now one was running the corinette. He loves to gamble and he get around to practice. He stopped practicing to go try to gamble. He didn't pay much attention to music. So finally, I don't know, he left Mobiliar. He's taking it up in his head and he's leaving some of the biggest orchestras in Chicago. And he's got his orchestras on. When I last heard from him about eight, ten years ago, he bought his mother a $30,000 home. You see? He's made good up there. What was his name? Cootie Williams. Oh yes, Chris Williams. Cootie Williams. He was with Duke Ellington a long time. Yeah, that's him. And I gave him one or two lessons, you know, what we called the Cowboys band. He didn't pull out on a comical parade, you know. And I gave him one or two lessons with Nolly Daniel. And he was one of them fellas that wasn't paying much attention, but now he got him all. He's famous now. And another boy, his name was Silas, and he disappeared all at once. The next thing we heard from him, he was over in England. And he'd done learning his clarinet and playing in Augustus over in England. What was his name? His first name was Silas, but I never did know him. Silas. Well, maybe we'll find out someday, his full name. But I don't know, he may be living now, but he left, and when we heard from him, he was over in England. And playing, and learned his clarinet. But those two boys, they didn't pay much attention when someone was trying to teach them. Especially Cootie, he loved to shoot crafts. Yeah. We'd be on jobs sometime, and when they'd have intermission, he'd go out there and find Cootie shooting craft. I'll tell you. He'd be intermission. But now he's got him orchestra, and they'd bought him his mother thirty thousand dollars.
Is folks still here, some of them, are they? Huh?
Or some of his folks? Yes, some of his folks are here. Yes, sir.
Well, I think that covers most of your life pretty well, unless you have something else that you wanted to add.

No, no more than, let's see, nothing. We don't want to keep you on there. You might put, take this on record, that at this present time, there's only three of those old, except the band, living. That's Johnny Polk, Willie Valera, and Dennis Tranger. In California. I think Mr. Polk told us of that too.
Yeah, he's okay.
All the rest of them is dead now.
Certainly feel honored to be able to talk to you and hear about this story. I've been, I've lived long enough to give you that information.
Well, thank you very much. Yes, sir. Yes, sir. Yes, sir.

segments.title: Opening: name, spelling and birth date for the tape
segments.summary: The interviewer gets Ballariel's name spelled and his birth date (11 October 1881) on tape; he is nearly 78.

segments.title: Creole Band splits and the Excelsior Band is organized
segments.summary: Ballariel explains the old Creole Band, Alexander Pope's breakaway to form the Excelsior Band, and that it lasted about 70 years.

segments.title: His instruments, joining the band in the 1920s, and its decline
segments.summary: He played strings by ear as a boy, learned brass as a grown man, joined the Excelsior Band in the 1920s and stayed 25-30 years as the old members died out.

segments.title: Serving as band secretary and keeping the job record book
segments.summary: He was appointed secretary and kept a book of jobs, pay and where they played, which settled arguments.

segments.title: Old band music: New Orleans Jazz and other parts handed over
segments.summary: Looking through his band music, they find New Orleans Jazz and other parts; he gives a piece to the interviewer.

segments.title: His 1950 heart attack and recovery
segments.summary: He says he nearly died of a heart attack about nine years ago but recovered.

segments.title: Bugle-call booklet, signing the music, and his address
segments.summary: They talk about a bugle-call booklet, he signs his name on the music, gives his address, and agrees to let the interviewer look at the record book.

segments.title: The ledger from 1917: baseball games, picnics and society jobs
segments.summary: The interviewer reads entries from May-June 1917 showing frequent small jobs for societies, picnics and lawn parties at low pay.

segments.title: Yearly bookings, more organizations and typical pay
segments.summary: Groups signed the band up a year ahead; the interviewer reads out more clients (clubs, shipbuilders, churches) and pay of about $2-4 a job.

segments.title: Pay for orchestras today compared with the old brass band
segments.summary: Ballariel says modern orchestras make far more than the brass band did, and brass bands have largely vanished.

segments.title: 1919 entries: Emancipation parade, balls and Mardi Gras dances
segments.summary: They discuss 1919 jobs, the band's own balls at carnival time, and playing for nearly every club or organization.

segments.title: Frequency of engagements and playing for baseball, football and races
segments.summary: The ledger shows a dozen or more jobs a month, nearly daily in May 1919; the band played for city-league ball games and horse races.

segments.title: Dance music of his boyhood: string bands, playing for nothing, and the family house
segments.summary: He describes string bands and early orchestras, playing mandolin, guitar and bass for fun, and dances held in his father's old house.

segments.title: Repertoire and dances: straight music, quadrilles, then fast jazz
segments.summary: The band started with straight music, waltzes and quadrilles; later came fast music, the shimmy and cutting-up, about 18-20 years ago.

segments.title: The Wise band of Pensacola and visiting bands
segments.summary: He recalls the Wise band from Pensacola, a prize-winning straight-playing brass band that swapped picnics with the Excelsior Band.

segments.title: Ragtime and mixed repertoire of the Excelsior Band
segments.summary: The band mixed ragtime and all kinds of time, and its reputation reached across the South.

segments.title: First hearing the blues, and the small bands he played in before Excelsior
segments.summary: Asked about the blues, he describes the Ponkinette and Lipscomb bands he played in, the Eureka band, and how Excelsior picked the best players.

segments.title: Cornet and alto in the Excelsior Band; clarinet and cornet types
segments.summary: He played cornet then alto in the band; they discuss saxophones and B-flat versus E-flat clarinets and cornets.

segments.title: Alexander Pope and the funeral of Ballariel's father
segments.summary: Alexander Pope had left the band before Ballariel joined, but the band played at the funeral of Ballariel's father when he was eight.

segments.title: How the band played funeral marches and the return from the cemetery
segments.summary: He describes society funerals: slow hymns, muffled snare drums, and livelier tunes like So Glad You're Gone on the way back.

segments.title: Funeral crowds, fights and the burial society uniforms
segments.summary: Big crowds followed funerals, sometimes ending in brick fights; he describes the societies' uniforms and the move of funerals to Sundays.

segments.title: Annual parades and the Mardi Gras ball on the wharf
segments.summary: They discuss yearly holiday jobs and the white carnival ball played on the municipal wharf on Mardi Gras night.

segments.title: The band's lineup, marching order, uniforms and night-parade lights
segments.summary: The fourteen-piece band also played dances; he explains instrumentation, marching formation, blue uniforms and the difficulty of reading music at night.

segments.title: Leaving and rejoining the band; the last three survivors
segments.summary: He briefly left the band, came back, and names Johnny Pope, himself and Denny Trainor as the old players still alive.

segments.title: Written music, the shimmy and playing the blues
segments.summary: The band always played from written music, added a little jazz, and played the blues; he explains the shimmy dance.

segments.title: New Orleans and other visiting bands
segments.summary: He recalls the Pickwick band visiting for picnics and does not remember the Sam Morgan band.

segments.title: Learning music: teachers in the band, and string instruments by ear
segments.summary: The band carried a teacher, and he learned strings by ear before learning notes on brass.

segments.chapter: Church, Creole life and Mobile musicians
segments.title: Church music, Catholic funerals and his father's funeral
segments.summary: He discusses Catholic funerals without band music inside the church and recalls his father, a laborer who died when he was about eight.

segments.chapter: Church, Creole life and Mobile musicians
segments.title: Creole language and the Creole people of Mobile
segments.summary: He talks about older Creoles speaking French, the broken French of Mon Louis Island, and his mother's and wife's French families.

segments.chapter: Church, Creole life and Mobile musicians
segments.title: Drums and basses in the early string bands
segments.summary: He explains that early string bands had bass violins and later a trap drum played by one man.

segments.chapter: Church, Creole life and Mobile musicians
segments.title: Cootie Williams and Silas, two Mobile boys he taught
segments.summary: He recalls Cootie Williams, whom he gave lessons and who loved shooting craps, and a boy Silas who later played clarinet in England.

segments.title: Closing: the three surviving old members and thanks
segments.summary: He notes only three old members remain, and the interviewer thanks him.
